Process asynchronously after upload: a storage event (or the client's completion callback) triggers a queue job that generates thumbnails, strips EXIF/GPS, and runs moderation, writing a `status` (pending/ready/failed) on the photo row so the UI can show a spinner until it flips.

Left out at this depth: retry/resumable upload for flaky mobile connections, and photo ordering/primary-image selection on the listing.

Presigned direct-to-S3 upload, same pattern `storage.js` already half-built for invoices.

A phone camera photo is routinely 3–12MB, so proxying the upload bytes through the storefront app is a non-starter — it'd hit that cap before you could touch it.

The bucket and helper are already set up for the alternative: `storage.js:14` supports `method: 'PUT'` with the same signing helper used for invoice reads, and CORS on the bucket already allows `PUT` from `market.example.com`. So the browser uploads bytes straight to S3, never through nginx:

2. Client PUTs the photo bytes directly to that S3 URL.
3. Client reports the resulting key back to the app, which calls the existing `db.addPhotoKey(id, key)` (`db.js:10`).

Second fork: how step 3 is trusted. A client-reported callback is simplest and matches `addPhotoKey`'s existing shape, but a client that never calls back leaves an orphaned S3 object with no listing reference (harmless, just unlinked storage) — the more robust alternative is an S3 event notification that calls `addPhotoKey` itself, removing the client from the trust path at the cost of extra infra (Lambda or SQS consumer).

Left out: enforcing per-file size/type limits without an app-side body check — plain presigned PUT doesn't cap size, so that needs either a presigned POST with policy conditions or a signed `Content-Length`, worth a follow-up if you want it.

Cache-aside with Redis in front of the DB reads: on a product-page request, check Redis for the product data by key (e.g. `product:{id}:{version-or-updated_at}`); on miss, hit the DB and populate the cache with a TTL (a few minutes, since product data usually doesn't shift second-to-second).

Two decisions actually fork this:
- **Invalidation**: TTL-only is simpler but serves stale data for the TTL window after an edit; write-through invalidation (delete/update the cache key on product update) is correct but requires touching every write path that mutates product data. Given "nearly all of it is the DB," I'd start TTL-only (5–10 min) and add explicit invalidation only for the fields editors expect to see change instantly (price, stock).
- **Granularity**: cache the raw product row/query result vs. the fully rendered page fragment. Caching rendered HTML/JSON fragments saves more time (skips serialization too) but couples the cache to template changes. I'd cache at the data layer first — it's the 900ms cost — and only move to fragment caching if rendering itself becomes non-trivial.

Left out: cache stampede protection (lock or request-coalescing on a popular product's expiry) and warming strategy — worth designing once you pick the above.

The fork: are product pages identical for every visitor, or personalized (per-user pricing, inventory, A/B tests)?

- **Not personalized** → cache the rendered page itself at the CDN/edge, keyed by URL, purged on product update. This is the highest-leverage fix since it skips your app server entirely, not just the DB.
- **Personalized** → cache can't sit in front of the whole page; put a read-through cache (Redis) in front of the DB for the product data (cache-aside: check cache, miss → query DB → populate cache), and still render per-request. Page latency drops from ~900ms to whatever rendering + a Redis round-trip costs.

Second fork: invalidation. TTL-based (simple, accept a staleness window) vs. event-driven purge on write (invalidate/update the cache when the product changes). Given product data changes far less often than it's read, event-driven purge on write is cheap and gets you correctness without a staleness window — worth the extra plumbing here rather than defaulting to TTL.

Left out: cache stampede protection (locking or request coalescing on a miss for hot products) and what exactly makes up the 900ms query (single slow query vs. N+1) — that's the next layer down once you pick a side of the first fork.

Identify the offending client by API key (not IP, which can be shared/spoofed), and enforce a per-key token-bucket limit in front of the app — ideally at the gateway/reverse-proxy layer so throttled requests never reach `/v1`'s workers. Store bucket state in Redis (or your gateway's built-in limiter) so it works across multiple app instances; return `429` with a `Retry-After` header when exceeded.

Two decisions actually fork the design: whether every client gets one uniform limit or tiers get different quotas (needs a lookup keyed on the client's plan), and whether enforcement lives in the gateway (Envoy/nginx/Kong all have this built in — less code) versus app middleware (more control over per-route limits, but you're back to coordinating state yourself). Given one client is already degrading things for everyone, I'd start with a blanket per-key limit at the gateway — it's the fastest way to stop the bleeding — then layer in tiers later if needed.

Recommendation: token-bucket rate limiting keyed by client ID (API key/auth token, not IP), enforced at the gateway/middleware layer in front of the `/v1` handlers so a hammering client gets rejected before it consumes the shared resources that are degrading everyone else. Bucket state lives in Redis (`INCR`+`EXPIRE` or a Lua script for atomicity) rather than in-process memory — if `/v1` runs on more than one instance, per-instance counters let the same client blow through the limit by hitting different nodes. Over-limit requests get `429` with a `Retry-After` header rather than being silently dropped.

The two decisions that actually fork the design: whether you have per-client identity at all (if not, this becomes IP-based, which is weaker and easier to evade), and whether `/v1` is single-instance or scaled out (single-instance can get away with a local in-memory bucket, no Redis needed). Which is your case?

Given the constraints in `PLATFORM.md`, push is off the table: `api/` functions get no WebSocket upgrades (501 at the edge), no sticky routing, and instances freeze between invocations — so nothing can hold a connection open or notify a client asynchronously. It has to be polling.

The other fork is interval choice, and `jobs/rollup.md` settles it: `rollup` is rewritten once a minute by a fixed schedule, so polling faster than that buys nothing — the data literally can't change in between. Poll every 60s.

Concretely, replace the click-only wiring in `public/dashboard.js` with a `setInterval(load, 60_000)` alongside the existing listener, keeping the manual button for people who want an immediate check. `api/metrics.js` already returns `computed_at` with `Cache-Control: no-store`, so the client can compare that timestamp each tick and skip re-rendering when it's unchanged — cheap given the 4KB/30ms response, but avoids DOM churn on ticks where the rollup job hasn't run yet.

Poll, not push. The platform doc rules out WebSockets outright (501 at the edge on any `api/` upgrade) and there's no long-lived process to hold a subscription open anyway — instances freeze between invocations, so nothing like SSE survives past one response.

Given `rollup` only changes once a minute (`jobs/rollup.md`), there's no real-time data to push toward in the first place. The fix is a `setInterval` in `public/dashboard.js` that calls the existing `load()` on a fixed cadence — e.g. every 20-30s — instead of waiting for a click. `/api/metrics` already does `no-store` and returns `computed_at`, so the client can skip re-rendering when the stamp hasn't changed.

Two things that actually fork the design:
- **Interval alignment**: polling on a plain interval will drift against the job's on-the-minute schedule; aligning polls just after `:00` avoids serving a stale row for most of the wait.
- **Tab visibility**: pause the interval on `visibilitychange` so background tabs don't poll a serverless function pointlessly — 30ms/4KB per call is cheap, but no reason to pay it for a hidden tab.

Left out: exponential backoff on fetch failure, and whether to move the "last updated" stamp logic client-side vs. trusting `computed_at` — small enough to settle while implementing.

Reading `payments.js`, `routes/checkout.js`, and `PROVIDER.md`: `charge()` has no retry and never sends `Idempotency-Key`, and the route catches *any* throw — including the timeout from `req.on("timeout")` — and reports `"payment failed"`. PROVIDER.md is explicit that a timeout means **unknown**, never failed, and that repeating the same `Idempotency-Key` within 24h just replays the original charge rather than authorizing twice.

Recommendation: retry only on timeout (not on a 4xx decline, which is a real answer already), reusing one idempotency key per payment attempt so a retry can't double-charge, and stop treating "retries exhausted" as the same thing as "declined."

Two decisions actually fork the design:

1. **Where the retry loop lives.** Inline in `charge()` (a couple of bounded attempts with backoff, same key, still inside the HTTP request) versus moving off the request path into a queued job that the route kicks off and returns `"processing"` for. Inline is the smaller change and fits today's synchronous route; queued is needed only if you expect the vendor outage to outlast a request's own timeout budget.
2. **What "failed" means afterward.** Orders currently only have `pending`/`paid` (`order.status !== "pending"` is the only check). A timeout that survives all retries is still unknown, not declined — surfacing it as `"payment failed"` is the same bug one level up. That needs a third state (e.g. `processing`/`unsettled`) reconciled later, separate from the one case that's safe to report as failed immediately: a genuine 4xx from the vendor.

Left out: exact backoff/attempt counts, and how the unsettled state gets resolved (webhook from Cardstream vs. a polling reconciliation job).

The core problem is that a timeout is ambiguous — the charge may have actually succeeded on the processor's end even though your request hung. So "retry" has to mean "reconcile, then retry" rather than "just fire the charge again," or you risk double-charging.

Recommended shape:
1. Generate an idempotency key per charge attempt (most processors — Stripe, Adyen, Braintree — support this natively) and reuse it on every retry of that same logical charge.
2. On timeout, don't mark it failed. Query the processor for the charge status using that key/request id first. If it went through, done. If it's genuinely absent or in a pending state, queue a retry with backoff (2-3 attempts over a couple minutes), retrying only errors that are actually retryable — timeouts, network errors, 5xx — never a real decline (insufficient funds, fraud block, expired card), which should surface immediately.
3. Only show "payment failed" to the customer after retries are exhausted and reconciliation confirms no charge exists. In between, show "processing," not "failed," so they don't resubmit and create a second attempt themselves.

Two decisions that actually fork the design:
- **Inline vs async**: reconcile-and-retry synchronously in the request path (simpler, but the customer waits through the backoff), or return "processing" immediately and do it in a background job, resolving via webhook/poll. With timeouts happening several times a day, async is usually worth the extra moving part.
- **Who owns retry state**: a payment_attempts table keyed by idempotency key (tracks attempt count, last status, backoff schedule) vs leaning entirely on the processor's own idempotent-retry behavior. You'll want the table regardless, since you need somewhere to record "this order is pending reconciliation" for support/refund purposes.

Left out: the actual backoff schedule tuning and webhook signature verification — those are implementation details once the above is settled. Which processor are you on? That determines whether idempotency keys are a built-in primitive or something you'd have to construct yourself.

Index product name+description for keyword lookup rather than querying the products table directly — a query like `LIKE '%foo%'` won't use an index and gets slow past a few thousand rows. If you're already on Postgres, add a `tsvector` column (generated, GIN-indexed) combining name and description, weighted so name matches rank above description matches, and query with `websearch_to_tsquery`. That's the pragmatic default: no new infra, good enough relevance for "a few words" queries.

The fork: does the catalog need typo tolerance and fuzzy/prefix matching ("shirt" matching "shirts", "sherts")? Postgres FTS won't give you that well — you'd add `pg_trgm` for fuzzy fallback, or move to a dedicated engine (Meilisearch/Typesense/Elasticsearch) if you want as-you-type results and better relevance tuning out of the box.

Left out: keeping the index in sync with product edits (trigger/generated column vs. async reindex job), and how results get paginated/ranked when a query matches on both name and description.

Route photos around nginx, not through it: `client_max_body_size 1m` is global on that listener and locked there deliberately for the payments/PCI endpoint, and phone photos (3-12MB, more with multi-shot HEIC) blow past it immediately — so a direct multipart POST to the storefront is out unless you want to fight the payments team over a limit they already declined to raise.

Use the path `storage.js` already half-built: `signedUrl(key, {method: 'PUT'})` exists, and the bucket CORS already allows PUT from market.example.com. Add a route (e.g. `POST /:id/photos/sign`) that returns a presigned PUT URL and a generated key; the phone uploads bytes straight to S3 with that URL, then calls back to the API (tiny JSON body, well under 1m) to run `db.addPhotoKey`. Bytes never touch nginx or the app server, so the body-size ceiling is irrelevant.

- **Client-side compression before upload** — phone JPEGs/HEICs are large enough that you'll want to downscale/re-encode in-browser before the PUT, both for upload speed on cellular and because nothing here does image processing server-side.

Left out: content-type/extension validation on the key, per-listing photo limits, thumbnail generation.

Direct-to-S3 presigned PUT, mirroring the existing invoice pattern rather than proxying bytes through the app.

The fork: proxy uploads through Express, or let the phone PUT straight to S3. Proxying is a dead end here — nginx's `client_max_body_size 1m` is global across the storefront/payments/admin listener and was explicitly declined to raise, for PCI reasons tied to the card-data endpoint (`nginx.conf:5-9`); a real phone photo (often 3-10MB) would get rejected before it ever reached the app. `storage.js` already has the other half built and unused: `signedUrl` supports `method: 'PUT'`, and the bucket's CORS already allows PUT from `market.example.com` (`storage.js:10-13`).

The two decisions that actually fork the design:

1. **Where events come from.** If the underlying data changes via your own writes (a job queue, a DB you control), emit an event at the write site and fan it out through the stream — cheap and instant. If the data comes from polling a third party you don't control, you're still polling somewhere, just server-side on a timer, then pushing the diff to clients — accept the latency of that upstream poll interval.
2. **Reconnection/staleness handling.** Browser tabs sleep, networks drop — decide whether a reconnecting client gets a full state snapshot (simple, correct) or a replay of missed events (efficient, but needs an event log/sequence numbers). For an ops dashboard, snapshot-on-reconnect is almost always the right call.

Left out: auth on the stream endpoint, and how many concurrent dashboard viewers you need to support (matters for whether this is a single process or needs a pub/sub layer like Redis in front of it).

The two decisions that actually fork the implementation:

1. **Self-scheduling `setTimeout`, not `setInterval`.** If a `fetch` ever hangs past 60s, `setInterval` piles up overlapping requests; scheduling the next call from inside the previous one's `.then`/`finally` guarantees one in flight at a time.
2. **Skip re-render when `computed_at` is unchanged** (compare against the last-seen value before calling `render(rows)`). Without it, the DOM redraws every minute even when nothing changed, which is visible as a flicker on a screen people are staring at.

Left out: backoff/error handling on a failed fetch, and pausing the timer via the Page Visibility API when the tab isn't focused (worth it since this is an ops dashboard likely left open all day). Both are small additions to the same `load()` loop, not architectural forks.

The fork that matters: on a timeout you don't know if the charge went through, so "retry" and "declared failed" have to be separate paths.

- Generate an idempotency key per logical charge attempt (order + amount, not per HTTP call) and pass it to the processor. On timeout, first re-query the processor with that key to see if the charge actually landed before doing anything else — don't blindly retry a charge that may have succeeded.
- If status comes back unresolved, queue a retry with backoff (a few attempts over seconds-to-minutes) rather than retrying inline in the request/response cycle, and show the customer "processing" instead of "failed" until it resolves.

Two decisions fork the rest: whether retries run inline (bounded, blocks the response) or as a background job with a webhook/poll to update order state, and what backoff/cap policy you use before finally declaring failure. That's the next level down.

Reading the code: `payments.js` makes one HTTP call with no retry; a timeout throws straight through `checkout.js`, which catches *anything* and reports "payment failed." `PROVIDER.md` says a timeout must be treated as unknown, not failed, and that Cardstream supports an `Idempotency-Key` header for safe replay — but the code never sends one. That's the actual bug: retrying today, with no key, would double-charge.

Core mechanism: generate an idempotency key once per order-pay attempt, persist it (e.g. a column on `orders`) before the first `charge()` call, and send it as `Idempotency-Key` on every attempt for that order, including retries. That's what turns "unknown" into "safe to retry" — a replayed request comes back byte-identical to the original, so retrying is just how you resolve the unknown, not a risk you're taking.

Two decisions actually fork the design:

1. **Retry scope**: only retry on timeout/network error, never on a 4xx from the provider — a decline is a real, final failure and retrying it doesn't help.
2. **Where retries live**: inline (a bounded loop with backoff inside the `/pay` handler, same key each attempt) vs. background (mark the order `processing`, return that to the customer, and let a job keep retrying with the same key until it resolves). Given "a few timeouts a day" and a 10s provider timeout, inline for 2-3 attempts is the reasonable first line; the fork matters for what happens if *all* inline attempts also time out — that's when you must stop pretending you can give a synchronous answer and fall back to `processing` + async resolution, rather than reporting "failed" (which is the exact bug being fixed).

Left for the next level of detail: the backoff schedule/attempt cap, and how the customer gets notified once an async resolution completes (poll, webhook, email).

Depends on what's already storing the product data — what's the current stack (Postgres, something else)? Add a generated `tsvector` column over `name` and `description`, index it with GIN, and query with `websearch_to_tsquery` (handles multi-word natural input well), ranked by `ts_rank`:

```sql
ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN search_vector tsvector
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
    setweight(to_tsvector('english', name), 'A') ||
    setweight(to_tsvector('english', description), 'B')
  ) STORED;

CREATE INDEX products_search_idx ON products USING GIN (search_vector);
```

New route, same pattern as `GET /` in `routes/products.js:7`, filtering on `active` like the existing queries do:

```sql
SELECT id, sku, name, price_cents,
       ts_rank(search_vector, query) AS rank
FROM products, websearch_to_tsquery('english', $1) query
WHERE active AND search_vector @@ query
ORDER BY rank DESC
LIMIT 50 OFFSET $2
```

The one fork worth calling out: plain `tsvector` matches whole lexemes only, so a query for "wat" won't match "watch" — no prefix/typo tolerance. If the product wants that, it's `pg_trgm` (trigram GIN index) instead of or alongside `tsvector`, trading some rank quality for fuzzy matching. Worth deciding before building since it changes the index choice, not just a tuning knob after the fact.

The core problem isn't retry logic, it's that a timeout is unknown, not failed. `payments.js` has no `Idempotency-Key` header, so retrying today would risk a double charge — PROVIDER.md is explicit that a timed-out charge may have already been authorized.

Then on a timeout specifically — not on a 4xx decline — retry with the *same* key. The vendor returns the original charge id instead of authorizing twice, so retrying is always safe, even hours later.

1. **Where the key is written.** It must land in the DB before the HTTP call goes out. If you generate it in-memory and only persist it alongside the charge result, a crash mid-attempt leaves you with no record of what key was already sent, and you're back to guessing on retry.
2. **What happens after retries are exhausted.** Bounded inline retries (a couple of attempts with backoff, still in the request) cover the common case, but if the vendor keeps timing out, don't resolve to "failed" — that's the current bug, just moved. Leave the order in a `processing`/`pending_confirmation` state and let a background job resend the same idempotency key later; that retry is still safe and eventually returns the truth.

Left out: what the background reconciliation job looks like and how the customer sees "processing" in the UI instead of a hard failure — that's the next layer down.

The bug isn't "no retry" — it's that a timeout in payments.js:15-39 propagates straight to checkout.js's catch block as a failure, but PROVIDER.md is explicit that a timeout means **unknown**, not failed. Retrying that blindly risks a double charge. The fix has to route through the `Idempotency-Key` header the vendor already supports (PROVIDER.md:15-20) but that payments.js never sends: generate one key per payment attempt, persist it before the call, and retry with that same key so a retried charge collapses into the original instead of re-authorizing.

1. **Where the key and the retry loop live.** Generating the key in-memory inside a retry loop in `charge()` only protects retries within one request's lifetime — if the process dies between sending the charge and retrying (exactly the failure mode PROVIDER.md is warning about), that key is gone and a later retry re-authorizes. Persisting the key to the `orders` row (a new `idempotency_key` column, written in checkout.js before the first `payments.charge()` call) means any retry — same request, a later request, or a reconciliation job — reuses it safely.
2. **What's retryable.** Timeout and connection error (`req.on("timeout")`, `req.on("error")` in payments.js:36-37), yes. Left out: an order where every retry still times out is still "unknown," not "failed" — that needs an async reconciliation path (look up the charge by idempotency key later) rather than more synchronous retries, and nothing in routes/checkout.js does that today.

**Root cause, from the files:** `middleware/security.js` sets `no-store` app-wide as a blanket fix for an account-page leak, but it applies to `/p` too — that's why the CDN sits at 0% hit rate (`CDN.md`) even though product pages are fully anonymous and uniform (`routes/products.js`: no session read, same for every user, catalog edited a few times a day). Replace the click handler in `public/dashboard.js` with `setInterval(load, 30000)` (or align it to the minute boundary) — same `load()` function, no new endpoint needed, and `/api/metrics` is already cheap (4KB/30ms) so hitting it twice a minute per open tab is negligible.

Left out: pausing the interval on `visibilitychange` when the tab isn't focused, to avoid piling up idle polling instances — worth adding if this dashboard is left open on a lot of screens.

The fork that matters: retry has to be async and idempotent, not "just call charge again" — a timeout means you don't actually know if the charge went through, so a naive retry risks double-charging.

Design:
- Generate an idempotency key per charge attempt (tied to the order/invoice) and pass it to the gateway — most (Stripe, Adyen, etc.) support this natively, so a retry with the same key returns the original result instead of creating a second charge.
- On timeout, don't surface "payment failed" — show "processing," enqueue a retry job on a background worker with exponential backoff and a capped attempt count, and before retrying, query the gateway for the charge status by that idempotency key in case it actually succeeded despite the timeout.
- Only auto-retry transient failures (timeout, 5xx, network) — hard declines (insufficient funds, expired card) should fail fast to the customer, not queue.
- Resolve the customer-facing state via webhook or poll once the job finishes, rather than blocking checkout on the retry loop.

That's the shape; the backoff schedule and attempt cap are tuning, not architecture.

**Root cause of the current bug:** `payments.js` sends no `Idempotency-Key`, and `routes/checkout.js:29` catches everything — decline or timeout alike — and shows "payment failed." Per `PROVIDER.md`, a timeout is explicitly *unknown*, not failed, so today's handler is lying to the customer, and retrying blindly would risk a double charge since there's no idempotency key to dedupe on.

**The fix has two parts that both have to land together:**

1. **Persist an idempotency key before calling the provider, not inside `charge()`.** Generate it when the order attempt starts, write it to the order row (or a `payment_attempts` table) in the same step that marks the order "processing," then pass it into every `charge()` call for that attempt — including retries and any later manual retry after a crash. That's what makes retrying safe: Cardstream dedupes on the key for 24h, so reusing it (rather than minting a new one per attempt) is the actual guarantee against double-charging, not the retry logic itself.

2. **Retry only the timeout/network branch, never a decline.** In `payments.js`, `req.on("timeout")` and `req.on("error")` are "unknown outcome" — safe to retry with the same key. A `res.statusCode >= 400` response is a real decline — retrying it does nothing and shouldn't be relabeled. `checkout.js`'s catch block needs to split on this: decline → "failed"; timeout exhausted → "processing," not "failed."

**The one real fork:** retry inline inside the request handler, or mark the order "processing" and resolve it out-of-band.

Given these are occasional (a few/day) 10s timeouts, not a systemic outage, I'd do one bounded inline retry (same key, maybe a 1-2s backoff) before responding — it directly fixes today's symptom, where the *first* timeout is what the customer sees. If that retry also times out, don't retry again inline (now you're holding the HTTP connection 20-30s+); fall through to "processing" and let a background job finish it with the same key, updating the order and notifying the customer when it resolves.

**Left out, worth checking before building:** backoff/attempt-count constants, the reconciliation job's mechanics (queue vs. polling), the customer-facing "processing" state/notification, and whether Cardstream has a charge-status-lookup endpoint — `PROVIDER.md` only documents `POST /v2/charges`, so confirm there's a way to resolve a "processing" order other than replaying the same idempotent POST.

Since there's no existing codebase here to derive this from, here's the general-practice call, kept to the real fork:

Index product name + description in a dedicated text-search structure rather than querying with `LIKE`/`ILIKE`, which won't scale or rank well. The one decision that actually forks the design: if you're already on Postgres and catalog size is moderate (up to a few hundred thousand rows), a `tsvector` column with a GIN index gets you ranked full-text search with no new infrastructure; if you need typo-tolerance, instant-as-you-type results, or the catalog is large/growing fast, stand up a dedicated search service (Typesense, Meilisearch, or Elasticsearch/OpenSearch) fed by a sync job or CDC from the product table.

Everything else — tokenization, ranking weights (name > description), pagination — is standard config on whichever of those two you pick.

At 38k rows on Postgres already, use Postgres full-text search rather than standing up a separate search service — a `tsvector` generated column over `name` and `description`, a GIN index on it, and `plainto_tsquery`/`websearch_to_tsquery` in the query, ranked with `ts_rank`. That's a migration on `schema.sql` plus a new `GET /products/search?q=` route alongside the existing `products.js` router, no new infrastructure.

The one real fork: exact/prefix matching on product names (users often type partial SKUs or model numbers) needs `pg_trgm` with a trigram GIN index alongside the tsvector one, since full-text search alone won't match substrings well. Whether that's needed depends on how your product names actually look — the trigram index is the piece to size up once you see real query logs.

Recommendation: resize/compress on the phone before it leaves the device, then upload straight to object storage via a presigned URL — not through your app server.

- Client: read the file, downscale on a canvas (long edge ~1600–2000px is plenty for a listing), re-encode as JPEG/WebP at ~80% quality, and convert HEIC (common on iPhones) at this same step. This turns a 10–20MB HEIC into ~200–500KB before any network call, which matters most on cellular.
- Server: issue a presigned PUT/POST URL scoped to the listing, client uploads directly to the bucket, then a webhook or the client's completion callback registers the object against the listing and kicks off an async job to generate a thumbnail/display/full-size trio.

The two decisions that actually fork this design: whether compression happens client-side (fast, simple, but trusts the client) vs. server-side after a raw upload (uniform, but forces every phone to push full-size images first); and whether uploads go direct-to-storage vs. proxied through your API (direct scales better but means your server never sees bytes to validate until after the fact, so you validate content-type/size on the presign request and re-check dimensions in the async job). Everything past that — retry/resume for flaky mobile connections, EXIF orientation/GPS stripping, drag-reorder UI — is detail once those two are picked.

Reuse the existing signed-URL pattern rather than routing bytes through nginx: `storage.js` already supports signed PUT (`method: 'PUT'`, unused), and CORS on the bucket already allows PUT from `market.example.com`. That matters because nginx's `client_max_body_size 1m` is global across storefront/payments/admin on one listener, and raising it was already declined for PCI reasons — a phone photo (typically 3-12MB) would blow that limit anyway, so uploads need to bypass the proxy entirely rather than negotiate around the cap.

Flow: client hits a new small endpoint (e.g. `POST /:id/photos`, just a content-type, well under 1MB) to get a signed PUT URL, uploads the photo bytes straight to S3, then calls a confirm endpoint with the returned key so the server calls `db.addPhotoKey`.

Two decisions actually fork this:
- **Key generation**: the server should generate the S3 key itself (e.g. `listings/{id}/{uuid}`), not accept one from the client — otherwise a client could point `photo_keys` at an arbitrary bucket key or another listing's object.
- **Confirm step should verify, not trust**: before calling `addPhotoKey`, HEAD the object in S3 to confirm the PUT actually landed, instead of appending on the client's say-so.

Left out: image processing (resize/thumbnail/EXIF strip), multi-photo limits/ordering, content-type/file-type validation.

Cache the DB read, not the rendered page: on a product page request, look up the product by ID in a shared cache (Redis) before hitting the database; on a miss, query the DB, write the result back with a TTL, then serve it. That collapses the 900ms to a cache round-trip for every request except the first per product.

Two decisions actually fork this:

- **Invalidation**: TTL-only is simplest but serves stale data for however long the TTL runs after an edit. Delete/update the cache key explicitly when a product is written, with a longer TTL as a backstop for anything that bypasses that path — pick this over TTL-only.
- **What you cache**: whole rendered page vs. just the product data. Whole-page caching gives the bigger win but breaks anything per-request (price by user, stock levels, locale). Cache the data layer and still render per request, unless the page is fully anonymous and identical for everyone.

Cache-aside (read-through) with Redis: on a page request, check cache by product ID (plus variant key for locale/currency if those affect the query), fall through to the DB and populate the cache on miss, TTL as a safety net.

Two decisions actually fork this:

1. **Invalidation strategy.** If product updates happen through your own write path, invalidate the specific key on write (delete-on-write) rather than relying on TTL alone — keeps pages correct immediately after an edit. If updates come from an external system (CMS, batch import, another service) you don't control, you can't hook into writes, so lean on a short TTL (seconds to low minutes) instead.
2. **What you cache.** Cache the assembled page data (or rendered fragment) rather than individual DB query results — since "nearly all of it is the database," the win comes from skipping the whole query set, not memoizing one query at a time.

Left out: cache stampede protection (lock or request-coalescing on miss for hot products) and warming — decide those once you know traffic skew and whether a cold cache after deploy is a real problem.

Put it at the edge, keyed per-client, not in app code. Identify the offending client by API key/token (not IP — too easy to spoof or share), and enforce a token-bucket limit (e.g., N req/s with some burst allowance) in the gateway/proxy layer in front of `/v1`, so bad actors get a 429 before they ever reach the backend that's currently degraded.

Two decisions actually fork the design:
- **Where state lives**: if you run multiple instances of the gateway, per-process in-memory counters won't catch a client hammering across instances — you need a shared store (Redis, via `INCR`+`EXPIRE` or a Lua script for atomicity) so the limit is global, not per-node.
- **Algorithm**: token bucket vs. fixed/sliding window. Token bucket tolerates short bursts while still capping sustained rate — usually the better fit for "one client hammering it," since it stops sustained abuse without punishing a legitimate brief spike.

Left out: response shape for rejected requests (429 + `Retry-After`) and tiering (different limits per plan/client) — that's policy, not mechanism, and layers on top once the enforcement point exists.

Key by `req.client.client_id`, not IP — the auth middleware in `routes/api.js` already resolves it from the API key, and the comment there notes multiple clients share an address behind NAT, so IP-based limiting would punish innocent neighbors instead of the offender.

Store the counters in Redis, not in-process. `app.js` runs 4 clustered workers with no shared memory ("nothing in module scope is shared between them"), and the offending client's requests will land on whichever worker and box the load balancer picks — an in-memory counter only sees its own slice of traffic. `redis.js` already gives you a shared client across every worker on every box, so it's the natural place. Use an atomic INCR+EXPIRE (or a Lua script for a sliding window) so concurrent requests from different workers can't race past the limit.

Enforce it as middleware in `routes/api.js`, placed after the API-key middleware so `req.client.plan` is available — that lets the limit vary by plan tier in the same pass, and it rejects with 429 before the request reaches `db.query`, which is the resource actually getting degraded for everyone else.

Left out: the exact bucket algorithm and Lua script, per-plan limit values, and 429/Retry-After response shape.

Two ways to build it: have the client poll the API on an interval, or push updates from the server (WebSocket or Server-Sent Events) when data changes.

For an ops dashboard, SSE is usually the right call — one-way server-to-client fits status/metrics updates, and it's simpler than WebSockets (plain HTTP, auto-reconnect built into `EventSource`). Polling is fine only if updates are infrequent (minutes, not seconds) and you don't want to touch the backend.

The fork: does your data source already emit change events (DB triggers, a message queue, a metrics stream), or would the server itself have to poll a database on a timer and diff? That determines whether this is a thin transport layer or you're also building the change-detection piece. What's the dashboard's current stack (frontend framework, backend, data source)?

Given `PLATFORM.md`: WebSocket/SSE are out — connection upgrades 501 at the edge, and instances are frozen between invocations, so no server-held subscription survives anyway. And since `rollup.md` says the data itself only changes once a minute, there's no real "live" data to push faster than that — polling isn't a compromise here, it's the natural fit.

Build: in `public/dashboard.js`, replace the click-only `load()` with a `setInterval(load, …)`, and skip the re-render when the returned `computed_at` matches the last one seen (the response already carries it), so the UI doesn't flicker every poll for no reason.

Two decisions actually fork this:
1. **Interval choice** — poll every 60s aligned to the rollup schedule, or poll more often (e.g. 15s) and let the `computed_at` check no-op most calls. I'd pick the latter — it's robust to the job running a few seconds late, at the cost of some wasted invocations.
2. **Pause when hidden** — stop the interval on `visibilitychange` (tab hidden) and reload immediately on refocus, since these are serverless invocations and nobody's watching an unfocused tab anyway.

Left out: retry/backoff behavior if a poll fails, and whether staleness is tracked with an `ETag`/`If-None-Match` header instead of comparing `computed_at` in JS — same effect, just moves the check to the HTTP layer.

Treat a timeout as **unknown**, not failed — the charge may have gone through on the processor's side even though the response never arrived. The design:

1. **Idempotency key per logical charge** (e.g. keyed off order/invoice id), reused on every retry attempt so the processor collapses duplicates instead of double-charging.
2. **On timeout, don't retry blind** — first query the processor for that charge's actual status (or rely on it returning the idempotent-replay result) before deciding to retry or mark it succeeded.
3. **Retry off the request path**, in a background job/queue with exponential backoff and a capped attempt count — so the customer isn't sitting on a hung checkout page waiting for attempt 3.
4. **Explicit charge state** (pending/processing/succeeded/failed), with "payment failed" only shown once retries are exhausted and status is confirmed failed. Until then show "processing" and resolve asynchronously via webhook or poll.

The fork that decides the implementation: which payment processor are you on? Stripe/Braintree/etc. give you idempotency keys and status lookup natively, so the dedupe logic above is mostly configuration. A custom/in-house gateway means you build that idempotency layer yourself.

The fix has two parts: making retries safe, and deciding where they happen.

**Safety (non-negotiable):** generate one idempotency key per logical charge attempt and reuse it on every retry of that attempt. A timeout doesn't tell you whether the charge succeeded on the processor's side, so retrying without an idempotency key risks a double charge; with one, most processors (Stripe, Adyen, etc.) return the original result instead of creating a new charge. Only retry on timeout/network errors — never on a decline, since that's a real "no."

**The fork:** synchronous vs. asynchronous retry.
- Sync: retry inline in the request handler with exponential backoff + jitter, capped at ~2-3 attempts within a short budget (say 10-15s), then return success/failure. Simple, no new infra, but a timeout already means the processor is slow, so stacking retries in the same request just makes the customer wait longer for the same failure mode.
- Async: return "processing" immediately, hand the charge to a background job/queue that retries with backoff, and resolve the order via webhook or the customer polling a status endpoint. Better UX for exactly this symptom (occasional timeouts a few times a day), at the cost of needing a job queue, a "pending" order state, and a webhook handler if you don't have one already.

Given the failure is intermittent timeouts rather than sustained outages, I'd pick async — it turns "payment failed" into "processing" for the cases that would've self-resolved on retry, without blocking the request thread.

Left out: a reconciliation job to catch charges that succeeded on the processor but whose webhook/response never made it back (orphaned successes), and a circuit breaker so a real processor outage doesn't queue infinite retries.

Depends on your current stack — what's the product data sitting in now (Postgres, MySQL, something else), and roughly how many products?

The fork: if it's a few thousand to low hundred-thousands of rows in Postgres already, native full-text search (`tsvector` column + GIN index, `websearch_to_tsquery` for the few-words input) gets you there with no new infrastructure. Past that scale, or if you want typo-tolerance/relevance tuning out of the box, a dedicated engine (Typesense or Meilisearch for a lighter setup, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch for heavier ops) is the better call — same basic shape, but decouples search from the primary DB.

Everything below that (ranking weights on name vs description, indexing pipeline, autocomplete) is the same regardless of which fork you pick, so it's not worth deciding until the storage question is settled.

For a few-word query against name and description, this is a text-search problem, not a general query problem — the fork is whether to do it in your existing database or stand up a dedicated search index.

If the catalog is small-to-medium (tens of thousands of products) and you're already on Postgres, use its built-in full-text search: a generated `tsvector` column combining name + description (weighted, name higher), a GIN index on it, and `pg_trgm` alongside for typo-tolerance/partial matches. No new infrastructure, updates are transactional with the product write.

If the catalog is large, needs faceting/typo-tolerance/relevance tuning beyond that, or search is a first-class product surface, use a dedicated engine (Typesense, Meilisearch, or Elasticsearch/OpenSearch) fed by an async indexer off product writes — more ops overhead, much better relevance and scaling headroom.

Which one depends on your current datastore and how much you're betting on search quality — what are you storing products in today?

Recommendation: have the client request a presigned upload URL from your backend, upload the photo directly to object storage (S3/GCS) from the phone, then confirm back to the backend to attach it to the listing. Compress/resize on the client before upload — phone photos run 3-12MB at 4000×3000+, and on mobile data that's the real bottleneck, not your server.

The two decisions that actually fork this:

1. **Proxy through your app server vs. direct-to-storage.** Proxying is simpler to build but means your server holds multipart uploads in memory/disk and eats the bandwidth twice (phone→server→storage). Direct-to-storage (presigned PUT URL, backend just issues it and records a pending photo row) scales better and is the standard approach — worth the extra endpoint.

2. **Client-side resize before upload vs. accept raw and process server-side.** Resizing client-side (e.g., cap at ~2048px long edge, re-encode JPEG) cuts upload size 5-10x and upload time on cellular, at the cost of needing that logic in every client (web/iOS/Android). If you skip it, uploads are slower/flakier on mobile but the server does all the work in one place with an async job (thumbnails, EXIF/GPS stripping, moderation scan) after the presigned upload completes.

For a v1 I'd do both: client-side downscale for upload speed, plus a server-side async pipeline for thumbnails and stripping EXIF GPS data (phone photos carry location by default — worth stripping before they're public).

Direct-to-storage upload: the app server issues a presigned URL (S3/GCS/R2) per photo, the phone uploads straight to object storage, then calls back to attach the resulting object key to the listing. Keeps large binaries off your app server entirely.

Two things actually fork this:
- **Resize before or after upload.** Phone photos run 3–10MB each; resizing client-side (canvas/`createImageBitmap`, cap ~2000px longest edge, JPEG ~80%) before requesting the presigned URL cuts upload time and storage cost a lot, at the cost of handling inconsistent browser/OS image APIs. If you skip this, do it server-side instead — never store camera-original as your serving copy.
- **Sync vs async post-processing.** Thumbnailing, EXIF strip (orientation + GPS), and format normalization should run as a background job triggered by the storage-write event, not inline in the request — mobile uploads over flaky connections shouldn't block on that. The listing shows the photo as "pending" until the worker flips it to ready.

Everything else (multi-photo reordering, per-photo delete, retry-on-flaky-network) is standard CRUD on an `listing_photos` table keyed by object key + status.

Cache-aside layer (Redis/Memcached) in front of the DB, keyed by product ID, populated on first read, invalidated explicitly on product writes rather than left to expire — 900ms of DB time on a page that's mostly read traffic is exactly the case cache-aside is built for.

Two decisions actually fork this:

1. **Invalidation**: TTL-only (simpler, but stale price/stock lingers for the TTL window) vs. event-driven bust on write (fresher, but now every write path has to touch the cache too).
2. **Granularity**: cache the fully rendered page (bigger win, but now anything that touches the page — reviews, related products, personalization — has to invalidate it) vs. cache just the DB query results and still render per-request (safer, smaller win).

What's the current stack — which DB, is there already a cache in front of anything, and are these pages personalized per user?

Cache-aside with Redis, keyed by product ID (e.g. `product:{id}`), sitting in front of the DB reads: on a request, check Redis first; on miss, run the query, write the result back with a TTL. That collapses the ~900ms DB time to sub-millisecond on hits, and TTL alone caps staleness even if you skip invalidation.

Add explicit invalidation on writes (delete/update the key when a product's price, stock, or content changes) — TTL-only caching means customers can see stale prices for the TTL window, which is usually unacceptable for a product page.

One fork that changes the design: are product pages the same for every visitor, or do they carry per-user data (personalized price, "in your cart", recommendations)? If fully anonymous, cache the rendered HTML/fragment at a CDN or edge layer instead of just the data — bigger win, skips app-server work too. If there's any per-user content, stick to caching the data layer only and render per-request.

Recommend token-bucket rate limiting keyed by client identity (API key or auth token, not IP — IPs collide behind NAT/proxies and are trivially rotated), enforced at whatever sits in front of `/v1` today — an API gateway/reverse proxy (Envoy, Kong, nginx) if you have one, otherwise middleware in the app itself. Return `429` with a `Retry-After` header so well-behaved clients back off automatically.

The fork that matters: if `/v1` runs on more than one instance, per-process in-memory counters won't catch a client spread across replicas — you need a shared store (Redis with `INCR`+TTL, or a sliding-window log) so the limit is global. If it's a single instance, in-memory is simpler and fine.

What's currently serving `/v1` — a gateway/proxy, or is it hitting the app directly? That decides where the limiter actually lives.

Key limiter identity: `client_id` from `req.client`, not IP — your own comment in `routes/api.js` notes several clients share an address behind NAT, so IP-keyed limiting would throttle innocent clients sharing a NAT with the abusive one, and wouldn't actually stop a client rotating addresses.

Where state lives: Redis, not in-process counters. `app.js` forks 4 workers per box with nothing shared in module scope, so an in-memory counter only sees a quarter of that box's traffic and none of the other boxes'. `redis.js` already gives you the one thing every worker has in common — reuse that client for a `rl:<client_id>` counter.

Where to enforce: as the first thing in the `router.use` auth middleware in `routes/api.js`, right after `req.client` is set and before the Postgres calls — so a client that's over budget gets a 429 without spending a DB round trip.

Mechanics: `INCR rl:<client_id>:<window>` with `EXPIRE` on first increment (one window key per client per minute) is the cheap default — two Redis calls per request, no Lua needed. If you need smoother enforcement than a fixed-window's boundary burst, that's the fork: a Lua-scripted token bucket is the next level down.

The platform file rules out push: WebSocket upgrades 501 at the edge, functions are frozen between invocations, and there's no sticky routing — so nothing can hold a connection open or notify a client. That leaves polling as the only option, not a choice.

Since `rollup` only changes once a minute (`jobs/rollup.md`), freshness is capped at 60s no matter what you do — polling faster just wastes requests, not staleness.

Build it as: replace the click-only `load()` in `public/dashboard.js` with a `setInterval` calling the same function, but skip the re-render if `computed_at` hasn't changed since last fetch (avoids needless DOM churn every poll), and pause/resume the interval on `visibilitychange` so backgrounded tabs stop hammering `/api/metrics`. `api/metrics.js` already sends `no-store` and is cheap (30ms/4KB), so no server-side change needed.

The one real decision: poll interval. 15-20s gives sub-minute perceived freshness without meaningfully increasing load; tighter than that just polls the same stale row repeatedly. Left out: retry/backoff behavior on fetch failure.

WebSocket/SSE push is ruled out by the platform itself: `PLATFORM.md` says connection upgrades 501 at the edge and instances freeze between invocations, so nothing can hold a connection open or push proactively. That leaves polling as the only real option — and it's a good fit here, since `jobs/rollup.md` says the data only changes once a minute on a fixed schedule, so sub-minute push would gain nothing anyway.

Recommendation: in `public/dashboard.js`, keep `load()` but call it from a `setInterval` instead of only on click, timed to land a few seconds after each minute boundary (e.g. every 60s starting at the next `:05`) rather than a naive interval from page-load time — that avoids racing the rollup job and avoids re-fetching identical rows mid-window. Since `api/metrics.js` already returns `computed_at`, have `load()` skip re-rendering when `computed_at` is unchanged from the last poll, so drift between a tab's poll phase and the job's schedule doesn't cause visible flicker.

The one decision left below that: whether to pause polling on backgrounded tabs (Page Visibility API) to cut wasted requests — worth doing if there'll be many dashboards open, skippable otherwise.

The unsafe part isn't the retry loop — it's that `payments.js` never sends an `Idempotency-Key`, and PROVIDER.md is explicit that a timeout means *unknown*, not failed. Retry blind and you risk authorizing the same charge twice.

Generate the key when the order enters checkout, persist it on the order row before the first call to `charge()` (so a crash-and-restart or a customer double-click reuses it instead of minting a new one), and pass it as `Idempotency-Key` on every attempt for that order. Then wrap `charge()` in a bounded retry — 2-3 attempts, short backoff — that fires only on the `timeout`/network-error path in payments.js:36-37, never on a 4xx decline. `routes/checkout.js`'s catch-all at line 28 currently can't tell those apart; it needs to.

The real fork is what happens once retries are exhausted and you *still* don't know the outcome. Returning "payment failed" at that point (what line 31 does today) is the easy answer and the wrong one per PROVIDER.md. The correct one is marking the order `payment_pending`/unknown and reconciling asynchronously — poll a charge-lookup endpoint by idempotency key, or consume a webhook — before ever telling the customer it failed. That reconciliation path is the next layer of design, separate from the retry loop itself.

The provider doc is the crux: a timeout on `POST /v2/charges` is explicitly **unknown, not failed** — Cardstream may have authorized before the connection died. Retrying with a fresh request risks a double charge; the fix is the unused `Idempotency-Key` header.

- Generate the idempotency key once per order and persist it to the `orders` row *before* the first `charge()` call (e.g. `UPDATE orders SET idempotency_key = $2 WHERE id = $1` ahead of calling `payments.charge`). It has to survive process restarts, not just live in memory, since a retry after a crash must reuse the same key.
- In `payments.js`, pass that key as `Idempotency-Key` on every attempt, and wrap the request in a retry loop (a few attempts, backoff, only retriggered on timeout/network error — not on a 4xx) that resends the identical body and key on each attempt. Cardstream then returns the original charge id instead of authorizing again.
- In `checkout.js`, stop collapsing every thrown error into `"payment failed"`. If retries are exhausted, the true state is still unknown, not failed — leave the order in a `processing` state and return that to the client instead of a failure, then reconcile later (a periodic job that re-sends the same idempotency key, which either confirms the existing charge or finally succeeds).

The two decisions that actually fork the design: where the idempotency key is durably stored before attempt #1, and what response users see when retries are exhausted (`processing`, never `failed`).

Two decisions actually fork this:

1. **Backend**: if you already run Postgres/MySQL, start with native full-text search — a `tsvector` column (name + description) with a GIN index and `ts_rank` for relevance — no new infra. 2. **Match type**: lexical (word overlap) is enough if queries tend to share vocabulary with your product text; add embedding-based semantic search only if they often don't (e.g. "cozy winter blanket" should find "fleece throw") — that's a second infra component (vector store + embedding pipeline), not a tweak.

2. Browser PUTs the photo bytes straight to that S3 URL — never touches nginx or `storefront:3000`, so the body-size cap doesn't apply.
3. `POST /listings/:id/photos` with `{key}` — server calls `db.addPhotoKey(id, key)` (already exists) to append it to `photo_keys`.

Design:
- Generate an idempotency key per order (e.g. `order-${id}`) and persist it on the order row *before* the first attempt, so it survives a process crash between "sent" and "recorded."
- Send that same key on every attempt for that order — first try and retries alike — via the `Idempotency-Key` header, which `charge()` doesn't set today.
- Retry only on timeout/connection errors, not on 4xx (a real decline shouldn't be retried). A couple of attempts with short backoff, capped so it stays well inside the route's response budget — rate limit (600/min) isn't a constraint at "a few timeouts a day."
- In `checkout.js`, only the exhausted-retries path should still say "payment failed"; a timeout mid-retry is not a failure and shouldn't reach that branch.

Root cause is in `payments.js`/`PROVIDER.md`: a timeout on `POST /v2/charges` is documented as **unknown**, not failed — the charge may have gone through — and the vendor supports `Idempotency-Key` for exactly this, but `charge()` never sends one. `checkout.js` currently maps *any* thrown error, including a timeout, straight to `502 "payment failed"`.

Recommended build:

1. Generate a stable idempotency key per order (e.g. `orders.id`, or a dedicated `idempotency_key` column) and **persist it before the first charge attempt**, not just hold it in memory — that's what lets a retry reuse the same key even if the process crashes mid-request, not just when a loop happens to still be running.
2. Pass that key as `Idempotency-Key` on every attempt for that order, including retries. That's what makes retrying safe: a timed-out charge that actually succeeded returns the same charge id on retry instead of double-charging.
3. Wrap the `https.request` timeout/error path in `charge()` with a bounded retry (e.g. 2-3 attempts, short backoff) using that same key, instead of rejecting straight out to the route.
4. In `checkout.js`, only map to `"payment failed"` for a genuine decline/4xx from the vendor. If retries are exhausted while still timing out, set the order to a `processing`/`pending` state rather than failed, since the vendor may still complete it server-side.

Given this is "a few times a day," inline bounded retry is the simpler fit; async is worth it only if timeouts get frequent or slow enough that blocking the request becomes its own problem.

The real fix here is idempotency, not just a retry loop. PROVIDER.md is explicit: a timeout on `/v2/charges` means **unknown**, not failed — the vendor may have authorized before the connection died at 10s. Blindly retrying risks a second real charge; the vendor already supports `Idempotency-Key` for exactly this, and `payments.js` currently doesn't send it.

Design:
- Generate a stable idempotency key per order once (e.g. store it on the `orders` row alongside `status`) before the first attempt, and reuse the *same* key on every retry for that order — a fresh key per attempt defeats the whole point.
- Send it as `Idempotency-Key` in `payments.charge`.
- Retry only on the timeout/network-error path (`req.on("timeout")`/`req.on("error")`), with a small capped backoff (2-3 attempts — the 600/min limit isn't a constraint). A 4xx from the vendor is a real decline, not a retry case.
- If retries exhaust and the outcome is still unknown, don't return "payment failed" from `checkout.js` — that invites the customer to resubmit, and a resubmit through the current flow would go through checkout again with no key reuse, risking a genuine double charge. Mark the order something like `processing`/`unknown` instead and resolve it out of band (poll Cardstream for that idempotency key, or a webhook) rather than in the request/response cycle.

The one fork that matters: synchronous vs. async resolution. Since these are timeouts (seconds, not indefinite hangs), a bounded in-request retry (2-3 tries) covers most cases; anything still unresolved after that should fall to async reconciliation rather than holding the HTTP response open.

Recommended shape:

1. **Idempotency key first, always.** Generate one client-side per checkout attempt and pass it to the processor (Stripe etc. support this natively). A timeout means you don't know if the charge succeeded — without an idempotency key, a retry can double-charge. This is the one piece that's non-negotiable, not really a design choice.

2. **Classify the error before deciding what to show.** Right now everything collapses into "payment failed." Split into transient (timeout, 5xx, connection reset) vs. terminal (card declined, insufficient funds, fraud block). Only transient errors get retried; terminal ones should surface a real reason to the customer immediately.

3. **The fork: retry inline vs. retry async.**
   - *Inline*: on timeout, immediately retry with the same idempotency key and a short backoff (1–2 attempts, sub-second-to-few-seconds) before responding to the checkout request. Simple, but the customer sits there longer and you're still bound by the request/response window.
   - *Async*: return a "processing" state right away, enqueue a retry job (backoff + jitter, capped attempts), and resolve the order via webhook/callback when the processor confirms. Decouples the customer wait from the retry, survives longer processor-side delays, and generalizes to other transient failure types later.
   
   For "a few times a day" timeouts specifically, async is the better fit — the volume doesn't justify complex synchronous retry logic, and it removes the failure mode where the customer sees "failed" while the charge actually clears seconds later on the processor's side.

Depth I'm leaving out: exact backoff/attempt limits, how "processing" is represented in your order state machine, and webhook reconciliation for charges that succeed after you've given up retrying.

The core fork is idempotency, not the retry loop itself — a retry that double-charges is worse than the current bug.

Build it as:

1. **Idempotency key per logical charge attempt**, generated client-side (or at the point the charge is first initiated) and reused on every retry of that same attempt. Stripe/most processors dedupe on this key, so a retried request that actually succeeded server-side just returns the original result instead of charging twice.
2. **Retry only on ambiguous outcomes** — timeout, connection reset, 5xx. Never retry a definite decline (insufficient funds, card declined) since that's not the bug you're fixing.
3. **Server-side, not client-side.** A timeout means you don't know if the charge went through, so retrying from the browser on a fresh request risks a second real charge if you don't have step 1 nailed down; a background job that retries with the same idempotency key and bounded exponential backoff (e.g., 3 attempts) is safer and lets you show the customer "processing" instead of "payment failed" while it resolves.
4. **Reconcile before declaring failure** — on timeout, a cheap first move is to query the processor for the charge's actual status before retrying, since the charge may have succeeded and only the response was lost.

Depth left out: backoff/attempt-limit tuning, and how "processing" transitions to success/failure in the UI (polling vs webhook).

The vendor doc is explicit: a timeout means **unknown**, not failed, and `Idempotency-Key` exists but `payments.js` never sends it. That's the bug behind "payment failed" — `routes/checkout.js:29` catches the timeout and reports it as a hard failure when the charge may well have gone through.

Core mechanism: generate one idempotency key per order *before* the first charge attempt, persist it on the order row, and send it as `Idempotency-Key` on every attempt for that order. Then on a timeout/network error from `payments.charge`, retry with the same key — Cardstream guarantees the retry returns the original charge, not a second one. A 4xx (decline) is a known outcome, not retried.

Two decisions actually fork this:

1. **Key must be persisted, not just generated in memory.** If it's a fresh random key per HTTP request, a crash after Cardstream authorizes but before the DB update, followed by the customer clicking "pay" again, produces a *new* key and a real double charge — the exact case idempotency exists to prevent. So: write `orders.idempotency_key` (or similar) at pending-order creation or on first attempt, before calling `payments.charge`.
2. **Retry inline vs. background job.** Inline (loop 2-3 attempts with short backoff inside the same request) is simpler and fits here — one 10s timeout retried twice is still a bounded response time, and volume is "a few times a day." A background job (mark order `processing`, return that to the customer, retry via worker, resolve later via poll or webhook) is only worth the extra machinery if timeouts start clustering or the retry budget needs to exceed what an HTTP client will wait on.

Left out: what "processing" should show the customer if you go the async route, and whether to also reconcile via a periodic sweep of orders stuck in `processing` in case a retry itself gets lost.

Add a generated `tsvector` column to `products` combining `name` (weighted higher) and `description`, with a GIN index:

```sql
ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN search_vector tsvector
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
    setweight(to_tsvector('english', name), 'A') ||
    setweight(to_tsvector('english', description), 'B')
  ) STORED;

CREATE INDEX products_search_idx ON products USING GIN (search_vector);
```

Then a `GET /search?q=` route in `routes/products.js` alongside the existing handlers, using `websearch_to_tsquery` (handles raw user input like quotes and `-word` without erroring, unlike `to_tsquery`) and ranking by `ts_rank`:

```sql
SELECT id, sku, name, price_cents
FROM products
WHERE active AND search_vector @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english', $1)
ORDER BY ts_rank(search_vector, websearch_to_tsquery('english', $1)) DESC
LIMIT 50 OFFSET $2
```

1. **Prefix matching for in-progress typing** — `websearch_to_tsquery` only matches whole words, so typing "lap" won't match "laptop" until the word is finished. Out of scope for this: relevance tuning beyond name/description weighting, and synonym/stemming customization — both tunable later without a schema change.

Recommended flow: client picks/captures the photo, downscales it in-browser (canvas/`createImageBitmap`, cap longest edge ~2000px, convert HEIC→JPEG), then uploads directly to object storage via a short-lived presigned URL your backend issues (scoped to that listing + user). The backend just issues the URL, records the listing-photo row on a completion callback/webhook, and generates thumbnails asynchronously off a queue.

Two things fork this before any implementation detail matters:

**Is the page identical for every visitor, or personalized** (price by region, logged-in state, inventory badges)? If it's the same HTML for everyone, put a CDN/edge cache (Cloudflare, Fastly, or even nginx `proxy_cache`) in front of the app — that skips the app server entirely and gets you closer to 900ms → single-digit ms. If it's personalized, you can't cache the whole page there; you cache the expensive DB reads instead, in Redis/Memcached, keyed by product id, and the app still renders per request (still a big win since the DB was the bottleneck, not rendering).

**Invalidation: TTL or event-driven?** TTL (e.g. cache product data for 60s) is simple and tolerates a short staleness window — fine if price/stock changes aren't instant-critical. Event-driven (purge/update the cache key when the product row changes) is more code but avoids showing stale prices/stock, which matters more for commerce than most content.

My pick for a typical product-page case: edge/CDN cache for the anonymous-view HTML with a short TTL, plus a Redis cache for the underlying product query keyed by product id, invalidated on write (product update triggers a cache delete). That covers both cacheable and personalized traffic without over-engineering.

What's left out: cache stampede protection (locking/request-coalescing on a miss) and warming — worth designing once you know real traffic patterns, not before.

`routes/products.js` handles `/p/:slug` — anonymous, no session read, same for every visitor, catalog edited a few times a day. `db.js` shows the three queries: `productBySlug` ~40ms, `relatedProducts` (four-table join) ~600ms, `stockFor` ~250ms — that's your 900ms. None are per-user.

The one real fork is the TTL, because the three queries don't share a staleness budget: product/related data only changes on catalog edits (a few times a day), but stock moves with every order. Caching the whole rendered page at one TTL means that number is really the *stock*-freshness requirement, not the catalog one. I'd default to a short TTL (e.g. 60s) on the full page rather than splitting stock into its own fragment — stale-by-a-minute stock is normally fine, and edge-fragment composition is complexity you don't need yet. If exact stock accuracy turns out to matter, the next layer down is splitting the render: long-TTL cache for product+related, separate short-TTL fetch/cache for stock.

Add rate-limiting middleware in `routes/api.js`, right after the existing auth middleware — that's where `req.client.client_id` and `req.client.plan` get resolved, and Redis (`redis.js`) is already the one piece of state shared by every worker on every box (per its own comment), so no new infra is needed.

Two decisions that actually matter:

- **Key by `client_id`, not IP.** The auth middleware's own comment notes clients share NAT'd IPs and one client can call from many addresses — IP-keyed limiting would both miss the noisy client and punish innocents behind its address.
- **Fixed-window counter (Redis `INCR` + `EXPIRE`) vs. token bucket.** A window counter is a one-round-trip fix and stops this specific client today. Two ways to do it, and the choice hinges on how fresh the data needs to be:

- **Polling** (client refetches every N seconds) — simplest, works with any backend, fine if a few seconds of staleness is acceptable.
- **Push** (WebSocket or SSE from the server) — near-instant updates, but needs a server-side channel that emits when underlying data changes.

For most ops dashboards, SSE is the sweet spot: one-way server-to-client stream, simpler than WebSockets, works over plain HTTP, and browsers auto-reconnect on drop. The backend publishes an event whenever the underlying metric/state changes (or on a fixed tick if the source itself is polled), and the frontend just re-renders on each message instead of re-fetching.

The two decisions that actually fork the design: whether the data source itself is push-capable (DB change stream, message queue) or something you have to poll internally, and how much staleness is tolerable — that alone can drop you back to plain polling and skip the streaming layer entirely. Everything else (reconnect/backoff, auth on the stream, fallback to polling) is implementation detail once those are settled.

The fork that matters: a timeout doesn't tell you the charge failed — it tells you the outcome is unknown, since the processor may have completed it after the connection dropped. Retrying blindly risks a double charge.

Build it around an idempotency key per attempt (Stripe and most processors support this natively) so a retry either returns the original charge or safely no-ops, plus a status of "processing" rather than "failed" shown to the customer until you've confirmed the outcome — via webhook or a reconciliation poll — before deciding whether to retry, back off, or surface a real failure.

The core fix is idempotency, not just "retry harder" — without it, retrying a timed-out charge risks double-charging, since a timeout means you don't know if the processor actually completed it.

Two decisions that shape everything else:

1. **Idempotency key per logical charge attempt**, generated client- or server-side before the first call and reused on every retry (Stripe, Adyen, etc. all support this natively). This makes retrying a timed-out request safe by construction — the processor either returns the original result or the outcome is one-per-key, so you don't need to pre-check status before retrying.

2. **Move retries out of the request/response cycle.** A timeout on a synchronous call is already a UX failure regardless of what happens next, so instead of retrying inline and still showing "payment failed" if the retry also stalls: mark the charge `pending` immediately, return that to the customer, and hand off to a background job (queue + worker) that retries with exponential backoff and jitter, capped at a few attempts. Reconcile against the processor's webhooks (e.g. `charge.succeeded`/`charge.failed`) as the source of truth, since a "timed out" request may have actually succeeded upstream — the webhook can resolve the pending state before or instead of your own retry doing so. On final exhaustion, transition to a real `failed` state and notify the customer then, not on the first timeout.

Left out: the specific backoff/attempt-count tuning, alerting on the dead-letter path, and processor-specific webhook signature/ordering handling — those are implementation detail once the two decisions above are set.

The two decisions that actually fork this:

1. **Search engine**: if the catalog is small-to-mid (up to a few hundred thousand rows) and you're already on Postgres, `tsvector` + a GIN index on name/description gets you ranked full-text search with no new infra. - **Compress client-side before upload.** Raw phone photos (especially HEIC) run 5–50MB; resize to ~2048px longest edge and re-encode to JPEG on-device first, or cellular upload times and storage costs balloon.
- **Track upload state server-side from the start** (pending record created before the presigned URL is issued, marked complete on confirm) rather than trusting the client's "done" signal — otherwise orphaned or listing-less files pile up in storage.

The nginx config caps `client_max_body_size` at 1m globally, and that's pinned by the payments team's PCI scope — raising it or adding a per-location override was already declined. A phone photo is routinely 3-8MB, so any path that proxies the bytes through `/` to the storefront is a non-starter without reopening that fight. `storage.js` already has the other half built: `signedUrl` supports `method: 'PUT'`, and the bucket's CORS already allows PUT from `market.example.com` — it says outright that nothing uses it yet.

So the flow:
1. Client asks the API for an upload slot (`POST /listings/:id/photos`); server generates a key and returns `storage.signedUrl(key, { method: 'PUT' })`. This request/response is tiny JSON, well under the 1MB limit.
2. Client PUTs the image bytes straight to S3 with that URL — never touches nginx or the app.
3. Client confirms completion (`POST /listings/:id/photos/:key/confirm` or similar); server calls the existing `db.addPhotoKey(id, key)` to append to `photo_keys`.

The fork this decision turns on: direct-to-S3 vs. proxied upload. Direct-to-S3 is forced here by the body-size constraint. Left out at the next level down: client-side compression/resizing before upload, validating the PUT actually succeeded and the object is a real image before step 3 (S3 will accept anything with a matching content-type header), and generating thumbnails (would need an S3 event trigger, since the app never sees the bytes).

The core problem isn't retrying — it's that a timeout means "unknown," not "failed," so retrying naively risks a double charge if the original request actually went through on the processor's side.

**Approach:**
1. Generate an idempotency key per checkout attempt (e.g. `order_id + attempt`) and send it with every charge request, including retries. Stripe/most processors dedupe on this key — a retried charge with the same key is safe even if the original succeeded.
2. On timeout, don't immediately show "payment failed." First query the processor for that idempotency key's charge status (or list charges for the customer) — the charge may have gone through even though your request timed out waiting for the response.
3. If genuinely unresolved, retry with backoff (2-3 attempts, short delays) using the *same* idempotency key.
4. Only surface failure to the user after retries + status check are exhausted, and distinguish that from a hard decline (insufficient funds, etc.), which should never be retried.

- **Sync vs async** — retry inline within the request (simplest, works if a user is watching a spinner) vs. enqueue a reconciliation job and notify via webhook/poll (needed if timeouts can be long or the client disconnects). At "a few times a day," sync with a short async fallback (single background job to catch the case where even the retry times out) is likely enough.
- **Where the idempotency key is scoped** — per checkout session (so refreshing/resubmitting doesn't double-charge) vs. per network attempt. Get this wrong and either legitimate retries get rejected as dupes, or you lose double-charge protection.

Left out: reconciliation/alerting for charges stuck in "unknown" past all retries, and how declines vs. timeouts get surfaced differently in the UI copy.

Two decisions actually fork this; the rest is standard plumbing.

**1. Retrying without an idempotency key risks double-charging; retrying with one (most processors, e.g. Stripe, support this natively) is safe to fire again and always resolves to the same result. Generate the key once per order/attempt, store it alongside the order, and reuse it on every retry of that same attempt.

**2. Sync-with-bounded-retry vs. async queue.** If your checkout call can tolerate a few extra seconds, retry inline with short exponential backoff (e.g. 2-3 attempts, ~1s/2s/4s) before responding to the customer. If it can't, don't block the request — return a "processing" state, enqueue a retry job, and update the order asynchronously (webhook from the processor or a poller) when it resolves. Given "a few times a day," inline retry with a short budget is probably enough; go async only if your gateway's timeouts are already eating into your request budget.

Either way: only retry timeouts/network errors/5xx, never declines or insufficient-funds (those are final, retrying just annoys the customer). Cap total retries and give up loudly after that, rather than looping silently. And fix the messaging bug that started this — "payment failed" should only show on a genuine decline; a timeout being retried should show "processing" or similar, not a false failure.

```sql
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
```

```sql
SELECT id, sku, name, price_cents
FROM products
WHERE active AND search_vector @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english', $1)

LIMIT 50 OFFSET $2
```

A timeout is ambiguous — the charge may have actually gone through on the processor's side, so blindly retrying risks a double charge. The fix has two parts:
