On timeout, the server should first re-query charge status via the idempotency key before assuming failure, then retry with backoff (e.g. 3 attempts, exponential) only for retryable errors (timeout, network, gateway 5xx) — never for hard declines (insufficient funds, do_not_honor, fraud), which should fail immediately and not enter the loop.

That resolves the UX bug too: don't show "payment failed" the instant the request times out — show "processing" and let the retry/status-check resolve it, so a request that actually succeeded downstream doesn't get shown as failed to the customer.

Left out: the actual queue/worker mechanics (sync retry loop vs. async job) and webhook reconciliation as a backstop — depends on your stack.

Read `payments.js`, `routes/checkout.js`, and `PROVIDER.md`. The key fact is in the vendor notes: a timeout is documented as **unknown**, not failed — and `checkout.js` currently maps every thrown error, timeout included, straight to `"payment failed"`. Worse, no request today sends an `Idempotency-Key`, so even a plain retry (automatic or the customer clicking again) risks a second real charge.

**Core mechanism:** generate an idempotency key per order pay-attempt and persist it *before* the first call to `payments.charge`, then send that same key on every retry — automatic or customer-initiated. That's what turns "unknown" into something safely retryable: with the key, a retry either returns the original charge (already succeeded) or completes it (never went through); without it, "retry" just means "charge again."

**Retry policy:** only retry on timeout/network error/5xx — those are the "unknown" cases. A 4xx from the provider (declined card, etc.) is a real answer and must not be retried.

Two decisions actually fork the design:

1. **Where the key lives.** It has to survive a process crash between "sent request" and "got response," so it can't be in-memory — it needs a DB write (e.g. a `charge_key` column on `orders`, written before the `https.request` call) that a later retry, including a fresh HTTP request from a reloading customer, reads and reuses instead of minting a new key.
2. **Inline vs async retry.** Bounded inline retries (2-3 attempts, backoff, same key) inside the route handler cover the "few times a day" transient case without architectural change. If still unresolved after that, don't force a verdict — flip the order to a `processing` status and resolve it out-of-band (reconciliation job or provider webhook) rather than either hanging the HTTP response or guessing "failed."

Left out: tuning the backoff/attempt count, the reconciliation job for orders stuck in `processing`, and a lock against two concurrent pay requests for the same order racing to generate different keys.

38k rows on Postgres 16 doesn't need a separate search engine — Postgres full-text search covers this. Add a generated `tsvector` column on `products` combining `name` (weighted A) and `description` (weighted B), a GIN index on it, and a new `GET /products/search?q=` route using `websearch_to_tsquery` + `ts_rank` for ordering, following the same pagination shape as the existing `/` route in routes/products.js:7-14.

The one fork worth calling out: plain `tsvector` matching only works on whole words, so a query like "wat bottl" won't match "water bottle" until the user finishes typing. If you want partial/typo-tolerant matches as they type, layer in `pg_trgm` (trigram index) instead of or alongside FTS. Which one depends on whether this is a submit-and-see search box or an instant/autocomplete-style one — that decision drives the rest.

Start with Postgres full-text search: a `tsvector` column over name + description, a GIN index, `ts_rank` for ordering, and `pg_trgm` alongside it to catch typos/partial words. That covers "type a few words, get matches" without adding infrastructure, and works as long as the catalog fits comfortably in the database (tens of thousands to low millions of rows).

The real fork is keyword vs. semantic: if queries are close to actual product words ("red running shoes"), lexical search is enough. If you want it to match intent past exact wording ("shoes for rain"), you need embeddings and a vector index (pgvector, or an external engine like Typesense/Meilisearch/Elasticsearch), which is a bigger lift — separate indexing pipeline, embedding model choice, re-ranking. I'd ship lexical first and add semantic only if search relevance complaints show it's needed.

Direct-to-S3 upload, not through the app server: `storage.js` already has an unused `PUT` branch on `signedUrl`, and the bucket's CORS is already opened for `PUT` from `market.example.com` — it looks built for exactly this and never wired up. That's forced by `nginx.conf`: `client_max_body_size 1m` is global across the storefront, payments, and admin listener, and a per-location override was already requested and declined by the payments team for PCI reasons. A phone photo routinely exceeds 1MB, so proxying bytes through the app server behind that listener is a dead end.

Flow:
1. `POST /listings/:id/photos/presign` — server makes a key like `listings/:id/<uuid>.jpg`, calls `storage.signedUrl(key, {method: 'PUT'})`, returns `{url, key}`.
2. Client PUTs the image straight to S3 with that URL, bypassing nginx entirely.
3. Client calls back `POST /listings/:id/photos {key}`, server runs `db.addPhotoKey(id, key)`.

The fork to get right: step 3 trusts the client's word that the upload happened. Either verify the object exists (`HeadObject`) before appending, or drive the DB write off an S3 event notification instead of the client callback — otherwise a forged `key` in that POST appends an arbitrary S3 path to someone else's `photo_keys`, and a dropped callback (tab closed mid-upload) leaves an orphaned object with no DB row either way.

Left out: enforcing content-type/size on the upload itself (a bare presigned PUT doesn't check what's in the bytes — needs policy conditions, presigned POST, or post-upload validation) and any resizing/thumbnailing of the phone-camera original.

**Recommended architecture:**

1. **Direct-to-storage upload**, not proxied through your app server. Backend issues a short-lived presigned URL (S3/GCS/R2) after checking the seller owns the listing; the phone uploads the file straight to the bucket. Camera photos run 3–15MB — routing that through your API server just to relay it to storage wastes server capacity for no benefit.

2. **Client-side downsize before upload.** Resize to something like a 2000px long edge and re-encode as JPEG (or send HEIC and convert server-side if you want the original quality preserved) before the upload starts. On mobile uplink, cutting a 12MB HEIC to ~1-2MB is the single biggest win for upload reliability and speed — the trade-off is a bit of client complexity (canvas/native resize) versus uploading full originals and eating slow uploads on real-world cellular. Pick client-side resize; server-side-only leaves sellers on 3G watching a spinner.

3. **Async post-processing.** On upload completion (S3 event or client callback), a worker generates the variants you actually serve — thumbnail, card, full-size — strips EXIF/GPS metadata (privacy — sellers' photos otherwise leak home location), and normalizes format. Listing shows a "processing" state until variants exist.

4. **Data model:** a `listing_photos` table (`listing_id`, `position`, `status: pending/ready/failed`, `original_key`, variant URLs) — not columns on the listing row, since it's a one-to-many ordered set sellers can reorder/delete.

Left out: retry/resume for flaky mobile connections, and moderation (NSFW/fraud scanning) — worth a follow-up if either matters for this listing type.

Cache-aside in front of the DB query, not a bigger rewrite: on a product-page request, look up the product (and its related data — price, inventory, reviews summary) in Redis by product ID; on a miss, hit the DB, write the result back with a short TTL (e.g. 30–120s), and invalidate that key when the product is updated. That collapses the 900ms to a cache read for the common case and keeps staleness bounded by the TTL even if an invalidation is missed.

The one thing that actually forks the design: are these pages the same for every visitor, or personalized (price by account, stock by warehouse, etc.)? If they're not personalized, full-page or CDN/edge caching is the bigger win and makes the Redis layer redundant for anonymous traffic. If they are, you're stuck caching at the data layer as above. Which is it?

The 900ms is nearly all `relatedProducts` (600ms, 4-table join) plus `stockFor` (250ms) — `productBySlug` is only 40ms, and none of it varies by user (routes/products.js:6-8). Meanwhile the CDN is already sitting in front of every request, already honors whatever `Cache-Control` the app sends, and is at 0% hit rate — because `middleware/security.js` slaps `no-store, no-cache, private` on *every* response app-wide, including `/p`. That blanket rule was the fast fix for a 2024 finding about `/account/orders` leaking into a shared cache; it was never scoped back down.

So this isn't a "build a cache" problem, it's a "stop defeating the one you have" problem: split `security.js` so the `no-store/private` block applies only to `/account`, and give `/p` a real `Cache-Control: public, max-age=…` (with `stale-while-revalidate` if admin edits shouldn't be instant). That pushes the identical, non-personalized product page onto the edge and removes the DB round-trip entirely for cache hits, rather than shaving latency off it.

Left for you to decide: the TTL (catalog edits happen "a few times a day," so anywhere from a few minutes to an hour is defensible without purging), and whether to actively purge the CDN on admin save versus just letting it expire.

On exceeding the limit, return 429 with a `Retry-After` header rather than silently dropping requests.

- **Per-client limit source** — a flat global limit is simplest but wrong here since one client is hurting others; you want a limit keyed to that client's identity/tier, which means you need reliable client identification on every `/v1` request (API key, not IP).
- **Hard reject vs. shed-and-queue** — token bucket + 429 stops the offender but does nothing for requests already in flight; if the degradation is from saturated backend resources (DB connections, worker threads), you may also need a concurrency cap per client, not just a request-rate cap.

Left out: burst allowance tuning, multi-region counter sync, and whether to also apply a global circuit breaker as a backstop — those are next-level-down details once the two forks above are settled.

The one thing worth deciding: whether to compare `computed_at` client-side and only re-render on change, or just re-render every tick — re-render every tick, it's 4KB/30ms per `metrics.js` and simpler than diffing.

Two platform facts from `PLATFORM.md` rule most options out: WebSocket upgrades 501 at the edge, and even SSE needs a connection held open past the 10s function kill — so no push-based approach is viable on this infra. That leaves polling. But `jobs/rollup.md` says the data only changes once a minute, on a fixed cron tied to finance close — so the fix isn't "poll instead of click," it's polling aligned to that cadence instead of a naive fixed interval.

Replace the load-once/click-to-reload pattern in `public/dashboard.js` with a self-rescheduling poll: after each `/api/metrics` response, compute the delay to just after the next minute boundary (a few seconds of buffer for the job to finish, plus small random jitter so every open dashboard doesn't hit the function at exactly :00) and `setTimeout` to the next poll, rather than a fixed interval. Compare the returned `computed_at` to the last one before re-rendering, since the job can run late or the dashboard can open mid-minute.

Two decisions actually fork this:
1. **Cadence** — fixed short interval (simple, but most polls are wasted since data updates once/minute) vs. minute-aligned with jitter (matches the real update rate, fewer requests). Given the fixed cron, aligned wins.
2. **Change detection** — rely on `computed_at` already in the JSON body (no server change) vs. add ETag/304 to `api/metrics.js` (saves the payload). At 4KB/30ms per `api/metrics.js`, that server-side optimization isn't worth it.

Left out: pausing polling on `visibilitychange` when the tab is backgrounded, retry/backoff on a failed poll, and cross-tab coordination via `BroadcastChannel` so N open dashboards don't each poll independently — all worth doing, all secondary to the scheduling change itself.

Recommended approach: generate an idempotency key per charge attempt and reuse it across retries, then move retries out of the synchronous request path into a background job with exponential backoff. On timeout, always retry with the *same* idempotency key — a timeout means you don't know if the charge succeeded upstream, and blind retries without dedup risk double-charging. The customer-facing state should be "processing," not "payment failed," until the job resolves; update the order via webhook or the eventual API response.

Only retry transient failures (timeouts, 5xx, network errors) — card declines and insufficient funds are terminal and should fail immediately.

Two decisions actually fork the design:
1. **Sync bounded wait vs. fully async job** — a quick poll-and-wait (few seconds, 1-2 retries) keeps the UX simple but still risks a slow request; a queued job + webhook/notification handles slow processors cleanly but requires the UI to support a "processing" state and a way to notify the customer later.
2. **Who owns the idempotency key and its lifetime** — generated client-side per checkout attempt (survives page reloads) vs. server-side per charge record (simpler but lost if the client retries a fresh request instead of the failed one).

Left out: the retry/backoff schedule tuning and reconciliation job for charges stuck in "processing" past a timeout threshold — that's implementation detail once the above two are picked.

The vendor doc spells out the fix directly: a timeout means unknown, not failed, and there's an `Idempotency-Key` header already available that `payments.js` never sends.

Two things actually fork this design:

**1. Idempotency key must be generated once per order and persisted before the first attempt, not per HTTP call.** Store it on the order row alongside `status`/`charge_id` (e.g. `idempotency_key`, set when the row moves out of `pending`). Every retry — inline or from a later reconciliation pass — reuses that same key, so a timed-out charge that actually succeeded on Cardstream's side gets deduped instead of double-charged. A key minted fresh per attempt defeats the whole mechanism.

**2. Only retry on timeout/network error, never on a 4xx decline** — a decline is a real answer, retrying it just re-declines. Given volume ("a few times a day") and the 600/min rate limit being nowhere near saturated, a few inline attempts with short backoff inside the same request in `payments.js` is enough; no queue needed. Wrap the existing `charge()` logic in a loop that catches only the timeout case and reissues with the same `Idempotency-Key`.

That path should leave the order in a `charge_pending` state (key already persisted from step 1) and tell the customer their payment is processing, rather than reporting failure — with a reconciliation job able to replay the same key later to resolve it.

Recommendation: add full-text search on the products table rather than standing up a separate search service first — Postgres `tsvector` (generated column over name + description, GIN index) covers "few words, match by name/description" well and avoids new infra. Reindexing is just staying in sync with the existing writes, no separate pipeline.

Two things actually fork this:
- **Current DB**: this only holds if the catalog is already in Postgres/MySQL. If it's not, or catalog size/query volume is large, jump straight to a dedicated engine (Typesense/Meilisearch/OpenSearch) instead of migrating later.
- **Relevance bar**: plain full-text search gives exact/stemmed matches. If you need typo-tolerance, prefix-as-you-type, or ranked relevance tuning, that's the point a dedicated search engine earns its keep over Postgres FTS.

Left out at this level: ranking/weighting tuning, synonym handling, and how reindexing behaves under bulk catalog updates.

**Direct-to-storage upload**: client asks your backend for a presigned URL (after checking listing ownership), uploads the photo straight to S3/R2/GCS, then confirms with the backend to create the photo record. An async worker generates thumbnail/medium/full sizes and strips EXIF/GPS metadata.

Two decisions actually fork this:
- **Resize before upload or after?** Phone photos run 5–20MB and are often HEIC — resizing/compressing client-side (canvas, ~2000px JPEG) before upload saves real bandwidth on mobile networks vs. uploading full-size and downscaling server-side.
- **Sync or async processing?** Either the client waits for thumbnails to come back, or the photo record is created immediately and shows "processing" until the worker finishes. Async is the better fit for spotty mobile connections.

Left out: upload retry/resume for flaky connections, moderation, and storage/CDN lifecycle — next level down if you want them.

Route uploads around nginx, not through it: `client_max_body_size` is capped at 1m globally, and per-location overrides were already declined for PCI reasons — reopening that isn't worth it for a feature that doesn't touch payments at all. Use presigned S3 PUT instead. `storage.js` already has the PUT branch of `signedUrl` sitting unused, and the bucket's CORS already permits PUT from `market.example.com` — this looks like it was set up for exactly this and never finished.

Flow: the app server mints a short-lived signed PUT URL for a given listing (must check the caller owns that listing — a signed URL is bearer-token equivalent, so this check is the only thing standing between "attach a photo" and "overwrite anyone's listing"), the phone PUTs the image straight to S3 with that URL, then the client calls back so the server runs `db.addPhotoKey` to append the key onto `listings.photo_keys` — already a `text[]`, already provisioned, currently empty. Reads reuse the same GET-signed-URL pattern the invoice route already uses.

Two decisions actually fork this, worth thinking through rather than defaulting: how upload completion gets detected (client callback after the PUT succeeds vs. an S3 event notification, which is more robust to a phone losing signal mid-upload but adds infra), and where size/type gets enforced, since phone camera photos can run 8–12MB and nothing here currently constrains that — client-side before requesting the URL, or a condition on the presigned request itself.

The 0% CDN hit rate is the actual cause: `middleware/security.js` sets `no-store` app-wide, but it was written for `/account/orders` (genuinely per-user, correctly must never be cached) and applied everywhere to close an audit finding fast. `/p/:slug` is fully anonymous — price, stock, and copy are the same for everyone — and the CDN already sits in front and honors whatever `Cache-Control` the origin sends. So the build is: scope `no-store` to `/account` only, and give `/p` a real `Cache-Control: public, max-age=…, stale-while-revalidate=…`. That alone removes ~900ms for any repeat request to a given slug, with no new infrastructure, since the caching layer already exists and is just being told not to cache.

Two decisions actually fork this:

1. **TTL vs. purge-on-edit.** Catalog edits happen a few times a day, so a short TTL (a couple of minutes) tolerates the staleness fine and needs zero coordination with the admin tool. Only build purge-on-save (admin tool calls a CDN purge API on publish) if editors need changes to appear instantly — that's real integration work the TTL approach avoids entirely.

2. **Stock's volatility doesn't match the rest of the page.** Stock, related products, and the product row are currently rendered together into one cached response. If stock can tolerate the same multi-minute staleness (plausible — in/out-of-stock rarely flips minute to minute), one TTL for the whole page is fine. If it can't, stock needs to come out of the cached fragment (uncached endpoint or client-side fetch for just that field), which is more moving parts.

Not needed for the first win, but worth naming: caching `relatedProducts` (the 600ms four-table join) at the query layer, e.g. Redis keyed by product id, would cut latency on cache misses and reduce DB load independent of the CDN — that's the next layer down once the header fix is in and you're looking at what's still hitting the DB.

Cache-aside with Redis in front of the product-page read: on a request, check cache by key (e.g. `product:{id}:{version_or_updated_at}`), and on a miss, run the DB query and populate the cache with a TTL. This kills most of the 900ms for repeat reads with minimal risk, since a cache failure just falls back to the current DB path.

Two decisions actually fork the design:

- **Invalidation**: TTL-only (simple, but stale data for up to the TTL window) vs. event-driven bust on product update (fresher, but requires wiring invalidation into every write path — admin edits, price/inventory syncs, etc.). If product data changes rarely relative to reads, TTL-only (a few minutes) is usually enough.
- **What you cache**: the fully-rendered page/API response (fastest, but couples cache to template/serialization changes) vs. just the DB query result (more flexible, less speedup since rendering still runs).

Left out: cache warming/stampede protection (e.g. locking or request coalescing on a popular product's miss) and where the cache physically sits (per-instance vs. shared Redis) — worth designing once you know read volume and how many app instances there are.

Rate limit by `client_id`, not IP — clients share NAT and one client is already identified by `req.client.client_id` right after the auth middleware in `routes/api.js:17`, so key the limiter on that, post-auth.

Use a Lua script (or `INCR` + `EXPIRE NX`) for a fixed-window or sliding-window counter per `client_id`, atomic to avoid races between workers hitting Redis concurrently.

Left out: per-plan limit tiers, 429 response shape/`Retry-After` headers, and whether to fail-open or fail-closed if Redis is down.

Key it on `client_id`, not IP — `routes/api.js` already resolves `req.client.client_id` from the API key before any handler runs (routes/api.js:17), and the comment above it says clients share NAT'd addresses and use multiple addresses, so IP-based limiting either over- or under-blocks the wrong party.

Poll, not push. `PLATFORM.md` rules out anything that needs a live connection: WebSocket upgrades 501 at the edge, functions get killed at 10 seconds, and instances are frozen between requests so nothing (SSE, a subscription) can stay open or emit later. That leaves client-side polling against the existing `/api/metrics` endpoint.

- **Short polling** (dashboard re-fetches every N seconds): simplest, works with any existing REST endpoint, fine if updates are infrequent or staleness of a few seconds is acceptable.
- **Push** (WebSocket or Server-Sent Events from the backend, firing on data change): near-real-time, scales better once you have more than a handful of viewers or sub-second freshness matters, but requires a connection layer and a way to know when data changed (DB triggers, a message queue, or the write path emitting an event).

The fix hinges on two decisions:

1. **Send `Idempotency-Key`.** It's supported but currently unused (`payments.js` never sets it). Generate one per payment attempt and persist it on the order *before* the first call — persisted, not regenerated per retry, so a retry after a process crash still reuses it and the vendor dedupes correctly.
2. **Don't resolve an exhausted retry to "failed."** A few inline retries with short backoff are safe here (600 req/min limit, nowhere near it), but if all of them time out, the true state is still unknown, not failed. That has to become an order status like `payment_pending`, shown to the customer as "processing," and reconciled later by re-checking the charge status via the same idempotency key (or a webhook) — not surfaced as `502 payment failed` the way `checkout.js`'s catch-all does now.

Left out: the reconciliation job/webhook implementation, and the DB schema change to store the idempotency key and a `payment_pending` status.

The core problem isn't "retry the request" — it's that a timeout means **unknown**, not failed, and you're not sending an `Idempotency-Key` (`payments.js:21-25`), so retrying today would risk a double charge.

Build it as: generate an idempotency key per order before the first attempt, persist it on the order row (so a retry — even after a process restart — reuses the same key), pass it through `charge()` as the `Idempotency-Key` header, and only retry on timeout/network error (not on a 4xx from the vendor, which is a real decline) with the same key and a couple of bounded attempts. The vendor then dedupes server-side regardless of how many times you resend.

The one fork worth deciding up front: retry synchronously inside the `/pay` request (simple, but the customer's request stays open through backoff) vs. mark the order `processing`, return immediately, and retry from a background job while the client polls. Given "a few times a day" and headroom on the 600/min rate limit, synchronous with 2-3 attempts is the simpler default; async is the move only if you expect timeouts to cluster or backoff to stretch past what a browser will wait on.

Two forks decide the shape here; the rest is standard plumbing.

**Direct-to-storage, not through your app server.** Client asks the backend for a presigned upload URL scoped to the listing, uploads the file straight to S3/GCS/etc. from the phone, then calls the backend to attach the resulting object key to the listing record. Phone-camera files are large enough (often several MB each, more for bursts of listing photos) that routing them through your app server just adds a redundant hop and ties up server bandwidth for no benefit.

**Resize client-side before uploading, not after.** Full-res phone photos (HEIC or JPEG, often 3–15MB) are much bigger than anything the listing UI will ever display. Downscale to roughly 1600–2000px on the long edge and re-encode as JPEG on-device before requesting the presigned URL — this is the fork that actually matters for "phone camera size," since sellers are frequently on mobile data and upload time/cost scales with what you send, not what the server later needs.

Backend then reacts to the object landing in storage (event trigger or the "attach" call) to generate the display-size derivatives/thumbnails asynchronously and mark the photo ready.

Left out at this depth: retry/resumable behavior for flaky mobile connections, and content moderation/virus scanning on the uploaded object — both are next-layer concerns once this shape is in place.
